note: Judgements from vendor pages fetched on the date shown, not benchmarks. A tool with 'not run' was scored from its documentation only.

groups.job: CRM (where won and lost deals are mirrored)

tools.name: HubSpot
tools.supported_in_pipecairn: Adapter written from the docs (contacts only)

fit.evidence: Does the job Pipecairn needs from a CRM (a contact record to mirror to); Pipecairn keeps its own pipeline so it does not need HubSpot sales features.

setup.evidence: A private app token is enough, but the portal steps came from a third party and are UNVERIFIED (docs/facts/hubspot.md).

reliability.evidence: Hosted by the vendor, so no upkeep for you; no uptime measurement was made, score is a judgement.

cost.evidence: Page says free for up to 2 users and 1,000 contacts with no time limit; paid tiers are per seat (page fetched 2026-11-23).

data.evidence: Data sits with the vendor; export was not checked, so the score stays modest.

integration.evidence: The adapter writes contacts through one endpoint and was never run against the real service.

fit.evidence: Holds people and companies and has an API; real field names for creating a person are UNVERIFIED, so fit is scored below HubSpot.

setup.evidence: Self hosting is Docker Compose with Postgres and Redis (GitHub page and docs fetched 2026-11-23); more work than a hosted account.

reliability.evidence: You do the updates and backups; the repo is very active (about 61,000 stars on its GitHub page) but young.

cost.evidence: The twenty.com page says self hosting the open source core is free; the hosted plans are per seat.

data.evidence: Your own server and database, nothing leaves it; the repo licence file says mostly AGPLv3 with a few commercial and MIT parts.

integration.evidence: The adapter and a mock server exist and are tested, but the real input fields were never confirmed.

fit.evidence: A table of leads works, but there are no deal stages or reminders built in, so it is a log more than a CRM.

setup.evidence: Share a database with an integration token; the shape is in the docs, but a newer API version may need a different id (UNVERIFIED).

reliability.evidence: Hosted by the vendor; no uptime measurement was made.

cost.evidence: Free plan costs nothing but is capped on blocks; the page did not make API access on the free plan clear (fetched 2026-11-23).

data.evidence: Hosted by the vendor, export not checked.

integration.evidence: The adapter writes pages and was never run live.

recommendation.beginner: Skip a CRM at first. Pipecairn's own pipeline is enough. If the client insists, use the free HubSpot tier.
recommendation.implementer: Twenty when the client wants to own the data and you can keep it updated, HubSpot when they already pay for it. Run the real field check (docs/03) before you promise a sync.
recommendation.cost_sensitive: Twenty self hosted or the free HubSpot tier. Do not pay per seat for a CRM that only receives mirrored contacts.
recommendation.open_source_when: Open source is the right call when someone will patch the server and run backups. It is the wrong call when nobody will, because a stale CRM is worse than a hosted one.

fit.evidence: Booking links are its core job and a free plan exists, but Pipecairn would need an adapter and the pricing page does not say which plans include the API (fetched 2026-11-23).

setup.evidence: Hosted; you connect your calendar and share a link.

reliability.evidence: Hosted by the vendor; no uptime measurement was made.

cost.evidence: Free plan has one event type; paid plans are per seat (page fetched 2026-11-23).

integration.evidence: No adapter exists, so Pipecairn cannot use it today.

fit.evidence: Same job as Calendly with slots and bookings in its API; the adapter books through POST /v2/bookings (docs/facts/calcom.md).

setup.evidence: Hosted is easy; the self hosting page we fetched says self hosting suits personal, non production use, so production self hosting is a bigger job.

reliability.evidence: Active project (about 50,000 stars on GitHub); the slots version header was inconsistent in two doc pages, a sign the docs move.

cost.evidence: A free plan exists and paid plans are per seat; self hosting has no fee (pages fetched 2026-11-23).

data.evidence: Self hosting keeps data with you, and its root licence file on main (read 2026-11-23) is the MIT text and names no exception, while the project describes an open core model with enterprise only features. Check the licence notes of the folders you self host.

integration.evidence: Adapter and mock are tested; the real service was never called.

fit.evidence: Creates the meeting event but has no booking page for the lead, so the person must be given times another way.

setup.evidence: You need an OAuth token and how to get it is not covered by the adapter (UNVERIFIED).

reliability.evidence: Google's own API with high quotas (10,000 requests a minute per project on the quota page).

cost.evidence: The quota page says standard use of the API is at no extra cost, with charges planned only for going over quota.

data.evidence: Data stays in your Google account.

integration.evidence: One endpoint (events insert), never run live.

recommendation.beginner: Cal.com hosted free plan. You only share a link and nothing needs installing.
recommendation.implementer: Cal.com for most clients, because Pipecairn can read open times and book. Use Google Calendar only to drop the event on the owner's calendar.
recommendation.cost_sensitive: Cal.com free plan plus Google Calendar events.
recommendation.open_source_when: Self host Cal.com only if you can run a production server; for most clients the hosted free plan is the safer way to use the open source product.

fit.evidence: Sends and receives SMS in the US; the same carrier registration duty applies to every provider.

setup.evidence: 10DLC brand and campaign registration is needed and carries fees (page says registration onboarding fees apply, amount not stated).

reliability.evidence: Large and long established; no measurement was made here.

cost.evidence: Per message segment plus a carrier fee plus a monthly number rental; the figures on the page change (fetched 2026-11-23, about $0.0083 per segment).

data.evidence: Messages and numbers sit with the vendor.

integration.evidence: No adapter exists, so Pipecairn cannot use it today.

tools.name: Telnyx
tools.supported_in_pipecairn: Adapter tested on a mock (signature checked)

fit.evidence: Sends with POST /v2/messages and signs inbound webhooks with Ed25519, both in docs/facts/telnyx.md.

setup.evidence: Same 10DLC registration as any US provider; the portal steps for keys are UNVERIFIED.

reliability.evidence: Reliability was not measured; score is a judgement from the docs.

cost.evidence: Pricing page lists about $0.004 per message part plus the carrier fee and $1 a month per local number, lower than Twilio's listed rate (fetched 2026-11-23).

data.evidence: Messages and numbers sit with the vendor.

integration.evidence: Adapter, mock and a real Ed25519 signature test; never run against the real service.

recommendation.beginner: Do not text on day one. Email and calls first; add texting after the carrier registration is approved.
recommendation.implementer: Telnyx, because the adapter exists and is tested. Registering the brand and campaign is the client's job and takes time, so start it early.
recommendation.cost_sensitive: The listed per message rate is lower at Telnyx, but registration and number fees are similar. The big cost is the time to register.
recommendation.open_source_when: There is no close open source replacement for business texting in the US, because delivery depends on registered carrier routes, not on software. We did not invent a match.

groups.job: Sending cold email and reading replies

fit.evidence: A cold email platform with sequences and a unified inbox; Pipecairn already does sequencing, so it would only be a sending route, and a public API is not confirmed on the page.

setup.evidence: Connect your own mailboxes and use its dedicated sending addresses (what-is page fetched 2026-11-23).

reliability.evidence: Vendor run; a beta Platform API was seen in a search result, so maturity is unclear.

cost.evidence: Monthly plans by email volume with a 14 day trial (page fetched 2026-11-23).

data.evidence: Leads and campaigns sit with the vendor.

integration.evidence: Only a recipe prompt exists, no adapter.

fit.evidence: It creates mailboxes and sets up DNS records and warmup, it does not send campaigns; it feeds mailboxes into a sender, so it is a partner of the next row more than a rival.

setup.evidence: Mailboxes and DNS records are automated (page fetched 2026-11-23).

cost.evidence: Priced per mailbox per month on the page (Google or Microsoft mailboxes, warmup extra).

data.evidence: Mailboxes are on your domains but managed through the vendor.

integration.evidence: Its mailboxes could be used with smtp_imap, but that was not tested.

tools.name: Your own mailboxes over SMTP and IMAP (Google Workspace, Gmail, Outlook)
tools.supported_in_pipecairn: Adapter tested on a fake mail server
tools.run: run on a fake server only

fit.evidence: Sends, reads replies, keeps the suppression list and daily caps in Pipecairn's own code, which is what a sender needs to do.

setup.evidence: You need a separate domain, DNS records and an app password (docs/facts/gmail.md); the steps are manual.

reliability.evidence: Deliverability and mailbox health are on you; Google's sending limit page says 2,000 messages a day per user (fetched 2026-11-23) and limits can change.

cost.evidence: You pay only for mailboxes and domains.

data.evidence: Mail stays with your mail provider and the lead list stays in your own database.

integration.evidence: Tested against a fake SMTP and IMAP server; never a real mail host.

recommendation.beginner: One normal mailbox on a separate domain through smtp_imap, a few messages a day. It teaches you the basics at the lowest cost.
recommendation.implementer: smtp_imap with several client owned mailboxes. Add a mailbox supplier such as InboxKit only when you need many mailboxes and can check its terms. SendKit only if a client already uses it.
recommendation.cost_sensitive: smtp_imap. The paid tools add features Pipecairn already has.
recommendation.open_source_when: Own mailboxes are the right call when you can watch deliverability yourself. If you send in large volume and need dedicated sending addresses, a paid platform may suit better. Pipecairn does not claim it replaces one. A closeness above 100 percent only means Pipecairn already does the sequencing, not that the route is better for deliverability.

fit.evidence: The long established signing product with a REST API (the developer page says more than 400 endpoints).

setup.evidence: Hosted; you upload a document and place fields.

reliability.evidence: Large vendor, no measurement made here.

cost.evidence: Per user plans with envelope limits, seen in a search result for the vendor's regional pages; the vendor pricing page itself returned an error on 2026-11-23, so UNVERIFIED.

integration.evidence: No adapter and no recipe exists in Pipecairn.

fit.evidence: Open source signing with an API on paid plans; the create document endpoints were not seen, so fit is a judgement.

setup.evidence: Self hosting works with Docker or one click hosts (GitHub page fetched 2026-11-23); more work than a hosted account.

reliability.evidence: You do updates and backups; about 15,900 stars on GitHub.

cost.evidence: Free plan is 5 documents a month with 10 recipients each; paid plans are per month (page fetched 2026-11-23).

data.evidence: Self hosting keeps documents with you; licence AGPL-3.0 per its GitHub page.

fit.evidence: Free plan has one public signing link and its own branding; Pipecairn does not call its API, you upload the contract by hand.

setup.evidence: Nothing to install; the steps in the handoff note are UNVERIFIED against the live screens.

reliability.evidence: Hosted by the vendor; no measurement made.

cost.evidence: Free plan with limits, and low one time prices for paid plans (page fetched 2026-11-23).

integration.evidence: A folder with the PDF and a note, no calls to the service.

recommendation.beginner: Breezedoc free plan with the handoff folder. It is cheap and nothing runs on your side.
recommendation.implementer: Breezedoc by handoff for small clients. For clients who want signing built in, write the Documenso adapter from the recipe and test it before you go live.
recommendation.cost_sensitive: Breezedoc, or Documenso self hosted if you can keep it updated.
recommendation.open_source_when: Documenso is the right call when you want signed documents on your own server. It is the wrong call when a client's lawyer asks for a named, widely recognised vendor, and then DocuSign is the safe choice.

tools.name: Vercel
tools.supported_in_pipecairn: Deploy guide for the web app only

fit.evidence: Runs the web app only; the API and worker must run elsewhere.

setup.evidence: Set the root directory to apps/web and include files outside it (docs/facts/hosting.md).

reliability.evidence: Large vendor, no measurement made here.

cost.evidence: Hobby is free with usage caps and Pro is per seat on the pricing page (fetched 2026-11-23).

data.evidence: Code and logs sit with the vendor.

integration.evidence: A guide and config were written, never deployed.

fit.evidence: Runs the API, worker, web app and database together from the Dockerfiles.

setup.evidence: Dashboard setup; its Config as Code files are deprecated, so use dashboard settings (docs/facts/hosting.md).

cost.evidence: A monthly plan fee plus metered usage for memory, CPU and traffic (docs page fetched 2026-11-23).

integration.evidence: Guide and Dockerfiles written, built and started by the CI workflow, never deployed to Railway.

tools.name: Hetzner Cloud server
tools.supported_in_pipecairn: Deploy guide, compose file, backup script

fit.evidence: A plain Linux server that runs the whole compose stack, same fit as Railway.

setup.evidence: You create the server, add an SSH key, set the firewall and install Docker (firewall details UNVERIFIED).

reliability.evidence: You patch the server and own the backups.

cost.evidence: Small servers are listed at a few euros a month (page fetched 2026-11-23).

data.evidence: Your own server, in the country you pick.

integration.evidence: Compose file and backup script checked for syntax only.

recommendation.beginner: Railway for everything, or try the offline demo on your own computer first. Nothing to patch.
recommendation.implementer: Hetzner with the compose file when the client wants low cost and data in a chosen country; Railway when you do not want server duty.
recommendation.cost_sensitive: Hetzner, if someone can spend an hour a month on updates and backups.
recommendation.open_source_when: A server you run is the right call when you will keep it patched. It is the wrong call when nobody watches it.

groups.job: Reading replies with a language model (optional)

fit.evidence: Reads replies the rules do not settle; live accuracy was never measured here (UNVERIFIED), docs/REPLY-READER-EVAL.md.

setup.evidence: Create a key in the console and set it (docs/facts/anthropic.md).

reliability.evidence: Hosted by the vendor; no measurement made.

cost.evidence: Billed per use; the pricing page was not fetched for this score, so it is modest.

data.evidence: Reply text is sent to the vendor.

integration.evidence: The model backend is wired and tested with fakes; never called live.

recommendation.beginner: Stay on the offline stand in while learning. It is rules, not a model, and the eval doc shows how limited it is.
recommendation.implementer: Turn on the live model for reading replies, keep the rules for opt outs and bounces, then measure its accuracy on the held out set before a client depends on it.
recommendation.cost_sensitive: Keep the stand in and read the inbox by hand, since a person already approves every reply.
recommendation.open_source_when: A self hosted open weights model is not supported by Pipecairn today, so no match is scored. If you write one, test it on the held out set first.
